title: Add explicit request timeouts to the yfinance/Stooq market-data provider calls
description:
Found while diagnosing why the ticker detail view (GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis) was very slow (conversation session, 2026-09-29): the cause wasn't IBKR (confirmed -- swing mode never touches ibkr_provider, and GET /api/ibkr/status stayed fast throughout). Yahoo Finance was rate-limiting this environment (confirmed directly: a fresh request to https://query1.finance.yahoo.com/... returned HTTP 429) after a burst of real requests. Neither YFinanceProvider nor StooqProvider sets an explicit timeout on its outbound HTTP calls (yfinance's own internal default is 30s per underlying call, unset/unoverridden by this app's provider code) -- and get_analysis/_compute_signal fetch daily OHLCV, weekly OHLCV, and extended data sequentially (three separate blocking calls per ticker), so a degraded provider can stack close to 90+ seconds of latency for one ticker. Because each of those runs on FastAPI's shared worker-thread pool and nothing cancels a request a client has already given up on, this compounded under this session's testing load into genuine resource exhaustion: the live dev backend process was directly observed holding 125 live threads, at which point even trivial, unrelated endpoints (GET /docs, a static page; GET /api/ibkr/status, no provider call at all) became unresponsive too -- confirmed by requesting them concurrently with a stuck request. For comparison, the identical fetch-analyse-zones pipeline run directly in a fresh Python process with a warm cache completed in well under 1 second, showing the cost is in the request-handling layer under load, not the computation itself.

This is a real, generally-applicable robustness gap (not specific to today's rate-limiting spike) -- any future Yahoo Finance outage, rate-limit, or network degradation will reproduce the same cascading slowdown for every user of this app, not just fail the one affected ticker.

checklist.step: Add an explicit, reasoned timeout to every outbound yfinance HTTP call in YFinanceProvider (yfinance's Ticker.history()/other calls accept a timeout= kwarg passed through to the underlying request -- confirmed present in the installed yfinance package's own data.py, default 30s per call today if unset). Decide and record (decisions entry) the chosen value, trading off failing fast under a real outage against not killing a legitimately-slow-but-working fetch.
Check whether StooqProvider's own HTTP fetch (_fetch_csv) has an explicit timeout today; add one with the same reasoning if not.

Research and decide (decisions entry) whether GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis's sequential daily -> weekly -> extended-data fetch (app/api/routers/stocks.py's get_analysis) should become concurrent, mirroring the ThreadPoolExecutor pattern this codebase already uses elsewhere for the same reason (app.api.day_trader_signal.compute_day_trader_signals_concurrently, app.portfolio.pricing's per-position concurrent fetch) -- so a slow provider adds its cost once per ticker rather than up to three times.

Verify a provider timeout surfaces through the existing DataProviderUnavailableError -> 503 path (docs/architecture/API.md), not as an unhandled exception -- this app's already-documented graceful-degradation contract for the data layer.

Tests: a mocked slow/hanging provider call that exceeds the new timeout, asserting it fails fast with the expected DataProviderUnavailableError rather than hanging -- no live network calls, per docs/architecture/Testing.md.

decisions.decision: Chose a 10-second per-request timeout for every outbound yfinance HTTP call (both `Ticker.history()`'s own `timeout=` kwarg in `YFinanceProvider._fetch`, and a session-level clamp -- see the next decision -- for `get_extended_data`'s `.calendar`/`.info`/`.insider_transactions`), matching `StooqProvider`'s pre-existing `timeout=10` (stooq_provider.py's `_fetch_csv`).
decisions.rationale: 10s gives both providers the same per-request budget, so a degraded source fails at a predictable, consistent latency regardless of which one is being called. Rejected 30s (yfinance's own current unset-default for `.info`/`.calendar`/`.insider_transactions`, per `yfinance/data.py`'s `get`/`get_raw_json`): that's exactly the value that, times the three sequential get_extended_data property fetches plus the daily/weekly `.history()` calls, produced this task's own ~90s+ incident -- keeping it would leave the root cause unfixed. Rejected a much tighter value (e.g. 3-5s): Yahoo's chart/quote endpoints can legitimately take a few seconds under ordinary (non-degraded) load, especially for the `.info`/`calendar` quote-summary endpoints, which are heavier queries than the plain OHLCV chart endpoint; a too-tight cap would turn normal peak-hour latency into spurious 503s, trading one reliability problem for another. 10s is generous enough to absorb that while still bounding the worst case to a small, fixed multiple of itself instead of an effectively unbounded stack.

decisions.decision: Implemented the yfinance timeout via two mechanisms: (1) pass `timeout=` directly on the `.history()` call (`_fetch`), and (2) a `_clamp_session_timeout` helper that wraps the underlying `YfData` singleton session's `.request()` method in place, reached via `Ticker._data._session` (private attributes), to cap `.calendar`/`.info`/`.insider_transactions` as well -- rather than building an app-owned `requests.Session()` and passing it to `yf.Ticker(ticker, session=...)`.
decisions.rationale: Investigated the installed yfinance package (1.7.0) directly: `.history()` accepts a `timeout=` kwarg (default already 10s in this version, contrary to the task description's blanket '30s per call' framing, which turned out to describe `yfinance/data.py`'s lower-level `get`/`get_raw_json`/`post` default rather than every call site) and passes it through to the actual HTTP request. But `Ticker.calendar`/`.info`/`.insider_transactions` (used by `get_extended_data`) are plain properties with no `timeout=` parameter at all in this version -- confirmed by reading `yfinance/scrapers/quote.py`/`ticker.py` -- so there is no public per-call override for them; they fall through to `data.py`'s 30s default today, and three of those calls stacking is the single biggest contributor to the ~90s incident this task exists to fix. A session-level clamp is the only way to bound them. Rejected building a fresh app-owned session and injecting it via `yf.Ticker(ticker, session=my_session)`: yfinance's `YfData` (the object that actually issues every request) is a process-wide singleton, so the *first* `yf.Ticker(...)` call in the process determines its permanent session -- if that first call ever passed a bare `requests.Session()`, it would replace yfinance's own curl_cffi-backed TLS/browser-fingerprinting session (`yfinance._http.new_session`, preferred specifically because it reduces Yahoo rate-limiting/blocking risk) for the rest of the process, making the exact 429/blocking problem this task is fixing *worse*. Reaching into the session yfinance already built for itself and wrapping `.request()` in place preserves that fingerprinting while still bounding every request. Accepted the cost of touching private attributes (`Ticker._data`, `YfData._session`) for this: `_clamp_session_timeout` and `_new_ticker` are both defensive (`getattr`/`AttributeError`-guarded, silently no-op rather than raise) so a future yfinance internals change degrades this specific extended-data protection rather than breaking every fetch -- `.history()`'s own inline `timeout=` is unaffected either way.

decisions.decision: Confirmed `StooqProvider._fetch_csv`'s existing `urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10)` (stooq_provider.py:110) is adequate as-is; no code change made to StooqProvider.
decisions.rationale: 10s matches the yfinance-side timeout chosen above, giving both data sources the same per-request budget. `urllib.request.urlopen`'s timeout already raises `socket.timeout`/`URLError` on expiry, which `_fetch_daily`'s existing broad `except Exception` already converts to `DataProviderUnavailableError` -- no additional error-handling change needed on the Stooq side.

decisions.decision: Converted GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis's daily/weekly/extended-data fetch from sequential to concurrent, via `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3)` in `get_analysis` (app/api/routers/stocks.py), resolving `.result()` in the same daily -> weekly -> extended order as the previous sequential calls.
decisions.rationale: None of the three fetches depends on either of the others, so running them concurrently means a slow/degraded provider now costs its ~10s timeout budget once per ticker instead of up to three times -- directly addressing the compounding-latency mechanism (three sequential ~30s-capable calls stacking toward ~90s) that produced this task's own incident. Mirrors the already-established, already-reviewed `ThreadPoolExecutor` pattern this same file's `get_indicator_history` uses for its own daily+weekly concurrent fetch (backend-indicator-history-performance), and the pattern `app.api.day_trader_signal.compute_day_trader_signals_concurrently`/`app.portfolio.pricing` use for N-ticker fan-out. Resolving `.result()` in daily-then-weekly-then-extended order (rather than, say, whichever completes first) preserves the exact pre-existing error-priority behavior (a daily failure -> 404/422/503 takes priority over a weekly/extended one) so no existing error-mapping test needed to change. Verified safe against `CachedDataProvider`'s SQLite-backed cache layer without any cache-layer change: `get_extended_data` already takes the same `self._lock` `get_daily_ohlcv`/`get_weekly_ohlcv` do (app/data/cache.py), which was already documented and reviewed as safe for exactly this kind of concurrent-caller addition when the daily+weekly pair was made concurrent for backend-indicator-history-performance.

decisions.decision: Fixed PR #360's needs_work finding by replacing GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis's `with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:` block with manual executor lifecycle management: `executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3)` followed by a `try`/`finally` where the `finally` calls `executor.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)` instead of relying on the context manager's implicit `shutdown(wait=True)`. `.result()` is still resolved in daily -> weekly -> extended order, preserving the exact same error-priority behavior (a daily failure takes priority over weekly/extended) that both the original sequential code and the first version of this concurrency fix already established.
decisions.rationale: `ThreadPoolExecutor.__exit__` unconditionally calls `shutdown(wait=True)`, which blocks until every submitted future completes before an exception raised by an earlier `.result()` call can propagate out of the `with` block -- pr-reviewer reproduced this directly on PR #360 (a stub whose daily fetch raised immediately still took ~3.04s to return its 404 because `get_extended_data` was sleeping 3s). `shutdown(wait=False)` returns immediately without waiting for in-flight futures, so `.result()`'s exception now propagates the moment it's raised, regardless of how long the other two legs take. `cancel_futures=True` (Python 3.9+) is included for correctness/future-proofing even though with `max_workers=3` == the number of futures submitted here, all three tasks start immediately on submission and none are left queued for it to actually cancel -- if a future edit ever oversubscribes this executor (more futures than workers), `cancel_futures` would then cancel the ones still queued. Rejected switching to `concurrent.futures.as_completed` with early-cancel-on-first-failure: because all three futures start immediately (queue-less with `max_workers` == submitted count), `as_completed` wouldn't stop the other two from running anyway (cancel() returns False once a future is already executing), so it would add complexity (reordering results by which ticket resolved first, then re-deriving the intended daily->weekly->extended priority for the actually-failed one) without fixing anything `shutdown(wait=False)` doesn't already fix more simply. Rejected fully serializing the fetch to eliminate the 'all three calls issued unconditionally even when the first would short-circuit' side effect entirely: that would give up the actual overlap benefit this task exists to provide for the common (all-succeed) case, and the reviewer's finding centered on the fail-fast latency delay, not on eliminating that overhead in the failure case -- the already-filed backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups task's own checklist doesn't ask for that either. Worker threads for the two still-running legs are not leaked: they are pool-owned, keep running to natural completion after `shutdown(wait=False)` (which only stops the pool from accepting new work and doesn't block the caller), and their results (if any) are simply never collected since nothing calls `.result()`/`.exception()` on their futures again -- confirmed no unhandled-future-exception warning is emitted either way. Verified with a genuinely discriminating regression test (`TestConcurrentFetch.test_fast_daily_failure_returns_promptly_despite_slow_other_legs`, tests/integration/test_stocks_analysis.py): mutation-tested by temporarily reverting to the blocking `with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) as executor:` form, confirming the new test fails (elapsed climbs to ~1.0s instead of staying under 0.5s), then restoring the fix and confirming it passes again. **This decision's own claim about the abandoned legs turned out to be exactly the bug PR #360's second review round found** (see the next `decisions` entry below): they are not, in fact, safe to leave running in the background, because they still shared the request's own `db` `Session`.

decisions.decision: Fixed PR #360's second needs_work verdict (the DB-session race between an abandoned weekly/extended leg and the request's own `get_db` teardown) by giving each of `get_analysis`'s three concurrent legs its own independently-scoped `DataProvider`/`Session`, instead of sharing the single `Depends(get_data_provider)`-injected instance across all three. Concretely: a new `app.api.dependencies.get_data_provider_factory` dependency returns a callable that, each call, opens a fresh `SessionLocal()`, wraps it in a fresh `CachedDataProvider`, and closes that session itself on `__exit__` -- entirely independent of the request's own `Depends(get_db)` session and of every other call this same factory has produced. `get_analysis` now depends on `get_data_provider_factory` instead of `get_data_provider`, and each leg's fetch runs through a new `_fetch_via_scoped_provider(provider_factory, fetch)` helper that opens/uses/closes its own scope. `get_data_provider` itself (the single-shared-instance dependency) is untouched and still used by every other caller (`get_indicator_history` in this same file, `enrich_positions_with_price`, `watchlist.py`, `portfolio.py`) -- see this entry's `rationale` for why those callers don't have this problem and shouldn't be switched. Also added: `pending`-dict bookkeeping in `get_analysis` so a leg whose `.result()` is genuinely never retrieved (abandoned because a higher-priority leg already raised) gets a `Future.add_done_callback`-based `logger.warning` if it later fails on its own -- the second, non-reproduced finding from PR #360's second review round (a real fetch failure on an abandoned leg was previously silently discarded with no log line at all).
decisions.rationale: The fundamental tension the second review round's finding exposed: `get_analysis`'s fail-fast requirement (round 1's fix) means the handler must be able to return before a slower leg finishes, but any leg that touches the request's own DB `Session` cannot be allowed to keep running after that `Session` might already be closed (`get_db`'s `finally: db.close()`, which runs on the request-handling thread as soon as the handler returns/raises). Those two constraints are only simultaneously satisfiable if the legs that might get abandoned don't share a `Session` with the request at all -- waiting for every leg to finish before returning (rejected: defeats the fail-fast requirement PR #360's first review round explicitly demanded) and giving each leg its own session (chosen) are the only two approaches that actually resolve the tension rather than trading one race for another; a lock/coordination-based fix (e.g. having `get_db`'s teardown wait on `CachedDataProvider`'s existing `self._lock`) was rejected too: that lock is per-`CachedDataProvider`-instance, private to `app/data/cache.py`, and `get_db` (in `app/db/session.py`) has no reference to the specific `CachedDataProvider` instance(s) a given request happened to construct -- wiring that coupling in would leak a data-layer-specific concern into the generic DB-session dependency, and still wouldn't help the *no-Session-at-all-until-the-lock-releases* problem, only reduce the race window. Checked whether this codebase already solves the equivalent problem elsewhere first, per this task's own instructions: `app.api.day_trader_signal.compute_day_trader_signals_concurrently`/`_fan_out_per_ticker` and `app.portfolio.pricing.enrich_positions_with_price` both use the *shared*-session-with-`with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) as executor:` pattern (implicit `shutdown(wait=True)`) -- safe for them specifically because they always fully wait for every fetch they start before returning (no abandon-on-error short-circuit), so `get_db`'s teardown never runs while any of their own futures are still in flight. That's precisely the shape `get_analysis`'s round-1 fix deliberately moved away from (to fix the fail-fast latency regression), which is what reintroduced this exact race via a different path than the one `CachedDataProvider`'s own docstring already documents from PR #231. Confirmed switching `get_data_provider` itself (rather than adding a second, narrower dependency) to a per-call-session shape would be the wrong scope: `tests/integration/test_portfolio_pricing_session.py` (and the real `enrich_positions_with_price` code path it tests) deliberately relies on the request's own position-query `Session` and `CachedDataProvider`'s cache-write `Session` being the exact same object (`expire_on_commit=False`, so a mid-loop cache-miss commit doesn't re-expire already-loaded `PositionORM` rows the caller's loop is still iterating over, avoiding an N+1 query pattern) -- switching that shared dependency to a per-call session would silently defeat that optimization for a caller that never actually had this task's abandoned-leg problem in the first place. Confidence the race is genuinely eliminated (not just made less likely), beyond static reasoning: (1) each `CachedDataProvider` a leg uses now owns a `Session` nothing else references or will ever close except that same leg's own `finally` block, on whatever thread runs it -- there is no other code path left that can call `.close()` on it, so the specific interleaving PR #360 reproduced (one thread mid-`_prepare_impl()`/commit while another calls `.close()` on the identical `Session` object) is no longer topologically possible, not merely rarer; (2) wrote a new regression test (`tests/integration/test_stocks_analysis_provider_session_race.py`) that exercises the real `get_data_provider_factory` -> real `CachedDataProvider` -> real `SessionLocal`/`Session` machinery end to end (only the outermost `YFinanceProvider`/`StooqProvider` classes are monkeypatched, so no live network call happens), reproducing the exact fast-daily-failure/slow-extended-data-leg scenario across 40 repeated iterations per run; (3) mutation-tested this new test against the actual pre-fix commit (072e748, PR #360's second-review-round code): 5 of 20 fresh-process runs (25%) reproduced the exact `sqlalchemy.exc.IllegalStateChangeError: Method 'close()' can't be called here; method '_prepare_impl()' is already in progress` pr-reviewer's review comment quotes verbatim, matching the reviewer's own reported ~30-40% rate; (4) ran the new test against the actual fix in this commit 55 additional times across separate fresh processes (2,200 total request iterations) with zero failures -- a real, if small, amount of confidence beyond a single passing run, given this is a race and a single green run proves nothing on its own. Full backend suite (1486 passed, 99.92% coverage), ruff, mypy, `scripts/check_profit_target_wording.py`, and `scripts/validate_tasks.py` all independently re-run clean; `backend/openapi.json` regenerated with zero diff (this fix changes no route/schema, only internal dependency wiring).

comments.summary: Non-blocking: get_data_provider_factory gives each of get_analysis's 3 concurrent legs its own SessionLocal()-backed Session/connection, on top of the request's own Depends(get_db) session -- up to 4x this endpoint's prior per-request DB connection footprint. The engine's QueuePool is pool_size=5/max_overflow=10 (15 total, backend/app/db/session.py -- no explicit sizing). Empirically tested this round (10-12 concurrent real requests to this endpoint, each with a provider sleeping 0.3-2s before its cache write, i.e. 30-36 simultaneous connection demands against the 15-connection cap): every request still completed successfully with no OperationalError/pool TimeoutError, just some queuing (elapsed scaled roughly 2x the per-leg sleep instead of failing) -- so this degrades gracefully rather than failing outright at the concurrency levels tested, and a concurrent write race between two legs (or two requests) hitting the same cache tables is already handled by _upsert/_upsert_extended's pre-existing IntegrityError/OperationalError-swallowing (PR #231). Still worth tracking: at high enough real concurrency (well beyond what this single-user/local app ordinarily sees) this could eventually hit the pool's default 30s checkout timeout. Filed as a checklist item on backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups rather than blocking this fix, which resolves a real, frequently-reproducible data-corruption/crash bug that is strictly worse than a theoretical exhaustion scenario under load this app isn't sized for.

review.notes:
Third review round, following two prior needs_work verdicts (round 1: fail-fast-delay bug from ThreadPoolExecutor's implicit shutdown(wait=True); round 2: DB-session race between an abandoned background leg and get_db's teardown, sqlalchemy.exc.IllegalStateChangeError on ~30-40% of runs). This round's fix (per-call-scoped DataProvider/Session via the new get_data_provider_factory, so each leg opens/closes its own independent Session) is architecturally sound and genuinely closes the race rather than narrowing it.

Independently re-verified round 2's specific race, both directions: (1) ran the PR's own new regression test (tests/integration/test_stocks_analysis_provider_session_race.py, 40 iterations/run) against the current fix 35 times total (20 + 15 in two batches) -- 0 failures. (2) Built a git worktree at the pre-fix commit (072e748, round-1's code -- the last commit before this round's factory existed) with a from-scratch venv (to avoid the editable install resolving to the wrong tree) and an adapted copy of the same race scenario (fast-failing daily leg, slow extended-data leg, real FastAPI/get_db/SessionLocal machinery, only YFinanceProvider/StooqProvider monkeypatched) -- reproduced the exact sqlalchemy.exc.IllegalStateChangeError: Method 'close()' can't be called here; method '_prepare_impl()' is already in progress on 4/25 runs (16%), confirming both that the original race is real and reproducible with my own harness, and that my reproduction technique is valid, before trusting the 0/35 result against the fix as meaningful. Cleaned up the worktree afterward (git worktree remove), leaving the shared working tree exactly as found (stash@{0}, pre-existing and explicitly not mine, untouched).

Read _fetch_via_scoped_provider and get_data_provider_factory's _live_scope directly (not just the docstrings): confirmed a leg's SessionLocal() is only ever opened once its ThreadPoolExecutor task actually starts running (cancel_futures=True only cancels not-yet-started/queued futures, and with max_workers=3 == 3 submitted futures none are left queued in practice) -- so a truly-cancelled-before-starting leg never opens a session at all, and every leg that does start is guaranteed to close its own session via _live_scope's try/finally regardless of whether fetch() raises, since @contextmanager propagates the exception through the generator's finally clause before it exits the `with` block. No session leak in either direction.

Verified add_done_callback-based abandoned-leg logging: Python's logging module is internally thread-safe (module-level lock around handler emission), and concurrent.futures guarantees a done-callback runs on whichever thread completes the future (or synchronously, in the calling thread, if the future is already done when added) -- no new race introduced by logging from multiple worker threads.

Confirmed get_data_provider itself and its existing callers (enrich_positions_with_price, day_trader_signal._fan_out_per_ticker, get_indicator_history's own separate ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2)) are untouched by reading the diff and grepping every get_data_provider call site -- all still use the single-shared-instance dependency with the safe fully-wait pattern. Confirmed error-priority (daily > weekly > extended) and round-1's fail-fast-latency fix both still hold: TestConcurrentFetch's two tests (including test_fast_daily_failure_returns_promptly_despite_slow_other_legs) pass, and the full 33-test daily/weekly/extended priority suite in test_stocks_analysis.py passes.

Independently re-ran: full backend suite (1486 passed, 99.92% coverage, gate 90%; 100% coverage specifically on the new app/api/dependencies.py code), ruff clean, mypy clean, scripts/check_profit_target_wording.py clean, scripts/validate_tasks.py clean (347 files), backend/openapi.json regenerated with zero diff (correct no-op -- no route/schema change). No frontend changes in this PR (gh pr diff --name-only: backend + docs/tasks only) -- steps 9/9a's browser walkthrough and e2e suite genuinely don't apply here, noted explicitly rather than silently skipped. Ran an ad hoc architecture-review pass against docs/architecture/Backend.md for the new get_data_provider_factory dependency: correctly placed alongside get_data_provider in app/api/dependencies.py (the module Backend.md already designates for this), no new external dependency, same SQLite/SQLAlchemy engine reused -- no architectural mismatch.

One new non-blocking finding this round (connection-pool footprint, see review.comments) added to backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups's checklist (still planned, depends_on this task) rather than duplicating a new follow-up task. Posted as a COMMENTED-type PR review (gh pr review --comment), not approve/request-changes -- per CLAUDE.md, never merging or approving this PR myself. Moving this task's file to docs/tasks/done/ and mirroring index.json per this accept.
